title: Prefix anchoring with temporal KV-journaling to reduce GPU fragmentation
creator: Priya Nair
description:
Problem: As long-running and interleaved workloads increase, GPU-resident KV cache slabs show steady fragmentation: small, semantically-equivalent prompt prefixes map to distinct slab allocations, increasing GPU memory pressure and causing higher eviction churn during continuous batching. Existing dedupe systems catch identical fingerprints but miss near-duplicate prefixes that could share KV anchors.

Proposal: Introduce a lightweight temporal KV-journaling layer that anchors recent prefix fingerprints with inexpensive similarity metadata (minhash signatures + length/boundary hints). On insert, the journal records: prefix fingerprint, minhash buckets, timestamp, and a compact anchor id. During lookup, we probe the journal for recent anchors with matching minhash buckets and validate by a fast, on-GPU Bloom/LM hash comparison before promoting to a shared slab anchor. Anchoring attaches a small indirection (anchor id) to requests instead of copying full fragments across slabs.

Goals:
- Reduce duplicate/resimilar prefix copies resident on GPU by 30-50% for conversational and assistant workloads.
- Lower eviction frequency for hot slots, improving 99th percentile token latency under bursty traffic.
- Keep additional CPU/GPU overhead minimal: journal maintained in RAM with compact entries; validation uses a single fused kernel call when needed.

Design notes and rationale:
- Temporal windowing: the journal keeps high-fidelity entries for a sliding 10 minute window and decays older anchors using exponential decay to avoid stale sharing across contexts. This balances reuse vs. correctness for session-scoped prompts.
- Similarity-first filter: minhash buckets (k=8) serve as a cheap filter to group likely matches. This reduces full validation attempts to <5% of probes in our microbenchmarks.
- Anchor compaction: anchors track reference counts and small usage histograms; offline compaction jobs consolidate low-cardinality anchors into canonical slab anchors to reduce fragmentation further.
- Safe promotion: anchors are only promoted to shared GPU-resident slabs after validation against an on-GPU short-hash (64-bit) to ensure byte-level match of key KV metadata; mismatches cause creation of a new anchor.
- Compatibility: Works with existing prefix fingerprinting; can be toggled per-tenant via config and rolled out incrementally with telemetry gates.

Implementation plan:
1) Journal prototype (RAM-backed) and minhash module (CPU) + unit tests.
2) Kernel: small fused validation kernel to check on-GPU short-hash and perform anchor indirection.
3) Integration with allocator: allow slab anchoring references and refcounting semantics.
4) Compaction worker that runs asynchronously to consolidate anchors and emit metrics.
5) Bench harness: replay traces (chat assistant + search prompts) to measure memory reduction, eviction rate, and latency.

Metrics to track:
- Unique GPU slab allocations per host over time (target -35%).
- Eviction rate per minute during 95th/99th percentile traffic spikes (target -25%).
- Average and p99 generation latency under continuous batching (no regression >5%).
- Additional CPU and GPU time per request due to journal probes (target <2% overhead).
- False positive anchor matches and resulting correctness incidents (target 0).

Rollout strategy:
- Canary on internal dev tenant with journal enabled, monitor memory & latency dashboards for 48h.
- Gradual enablement by tenant cohort with circuit breakers: memory anomaly, latency error, or correctness alerts.
- If anchor compaction causes regression, revert compaction only while keeping live anchors.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Risk of stale anchors being used for semantically different prompts if temporal window too long; mitigated by on-GPU short-hash validation and short default window.
- Extra metadata increases RAM usage on control plane hosts; kept minimal by compaction and decay.
- Complexity in allocator and refcounting could introduce subtle memory leaks; will instrument strong invariants and leak detectors.

Documentation links:
- Design doc (internal Drive): https://drive.internal.redwood/d/1_prefix-anchoring-journal
- Benchmark harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-bench/tree/prefix-anchoring
- Related tickets: ENG-31245 (prompt-shadow-indexing), ENG-61234 (prefix atlas compaction)
acceptance_criteria: Journal can be toggled per-tenant via config flag
Bench harness shows >=30% reduction in duplicate GPU slab allocations on assistant traces
p99 token latency does not regress more than 5% in continuous batching scenarios
Anchor promotion validation kernel passes correctness fuzz tests
No memory leaks detected in allocator integration during 72h soak test

2026-03-07 - Bench run (internal assistant trace v3): unique slab allocations decreased 33% on a 48h replay; eviction rate down 22% during bursty windows. CPU overhead measured at 1.6% extra per request. Promising but need wider soak.

2026-03-10 - Oliver Chen: Noted a corner-case race between compaction worker and concurrent refcount updates; added CAS-based guard and new invariant checks. Pushed tests covering the race.

notes: This ticket focuses on short-term, high-impact reducer for GPU fragmentation. Larger long-term dedupe (cross-model canonicalization) should be tracked separately.
